note: General explanations by function for controls no guide explains (War Thunder, Nuclear Option, Star Citizen, the long tail). The first template whose words appear in the control's name (or the catalog's note) is used; {name} is the control's own name. Shown as a general description.

templates.text: "{name}" is a light: it tells the pilot that something is on, or that something is wrong.
templates.context: Pilots look for lit warning and caution lights all the time; a new light means: check what it says.

templates.text: "{name}" raises and lowers the landing gear: the wheels and their legs. They come down for landing and fold away in flight so the aircraft flies faster and smoother.
templates.context: The gear goes up soon after take-off and down before landing; lights usually show when it is down and locked.

templates.text: "{name}" moves the flaps: parts of the wing that slide out to give more lift at low speed.
templates.context: Pilots use them for take-off and landing; at high speed they stay in, or they could be damaged.

templates.text: "{name}" opens panels into the wind that slow the aircraft down, like opening a big umbrella behind a bicycle.
templates.context: Pilots use it to lose speed quickly, in a dive, when catching up too fast or before landing.

templates.text: "{name}" works the wheel brakes, like the brakes of a car, to slow down or hold still on the ground.
templates.context: They are used after landing, while taxiing and to stand still before take-off.

templates.text: "{name}" sets how hard the engine works: forward for more power, back for less, like the gas pedal of a car.
templates.context: It is used all the time in flight; full power for take-off and climbs, less for cruising and landing.

templates.text: "{name}" sets how much fuel goes into the engine's air. High up, where the air is thinner, the engine needs less fuel.
templates.context: On piston engines the pilot leans it out when climbing and enriches it for landing.

templates.text: "{name}" sets how sharply the propeller blades bite the air, which changes how fast the engine turns.
templates.context: High speed of turning gives the most power for take-off and climb; less is used for cruising to save fuel.

templates.text: "{name}" opens or closes doors that let cooling air through the engine or its radiator, so the engine does not get too hot.
templates.context: More open cools better but slows the aircraft a little; pilots open it on the ground and in climbs.

templates.text: "{name}" works the pump that pushes more air into the engine, so it keeps its power high up where the air is thin.
templates.context: Pilots switch it to the higher stage when climbing above a certain height.

templates.text: "{name}" switches the sparks that make the engine's fuel burn. Without it the engine cannot run.
templates.context: It is part of the engine start; switching it off stops the engine.

templates.text: "{name}" starts the engine: a helper spins it until it can run by itself, like the key of a car.
templates.context: It is one of the first steps before flight, after the electrics and the fuel are on.

templates.text: "{name}" belongs to the fuel system: it lets fuel flow from the tanks to the engine, or chooses or shows which tank is used.
templates.context: Fuel must flow before the engine can start; pilots watch how much is left during the whole flight.

templates.text: "{name}" belongs to the electrical system, the aircraft's electricity: where it comes from and whether it is on.
templates.context: Most instruments, radios and lights need it, so it is switched on first and off last.

templates.text: "{name}" trims the aircraft: small adjustments so it flies straight by itself without the pilot holding the stick.
templates.context: Pilots trim after every change of speed or power, so their hands are free and the flight is calm.

templates.text: "{name}" steers the aircraft: pushing and pulling moves the nose down and up, tilting it rolls the wings.
templates.context: It is the control used all the time in flight, held in the pilot's hand.

templates.text: "{name}" turns the nose left and right with the feet, using the rudder at the tail.
templates.context: Pilots use it to keep the aircraft straight on the runway and to fly turns cleanly.

templates.text: "{name}" makes the helicopter climb or sink by changing how hard the main rotor pushes.
templates.context: It is held in the pilot's left hand all the time in flight.

templates.text: "{name}" fires the guns or belongs to them.
templates.context: The guns only fire when the weapons are armed; pilots use them in combat and practice.

templates.text: "{name}" belongs to the weapons: it selects, arms or releases bombs, rockets or missiles.
templates.context: Weapons work only when armed; pilots select them before reaching the target.

templates.text: "{name}" is a safety switch for the weapons: while it is off, nothing fires or drops.
templates.context: Pilots switch it on only when a fight or a target is near, and off again afterwards.

templates.text: "{name}" drops weapons or extra tanks in an emergency, to make the aircraft lighter.
templates.context: It is used when the aircraft must become light and fast at once, for example to escape.

templates.text: "{name}" belongs to the sight: the aiming mark the pilot looks through to point weapons at a target.
templates.context: Its brightness and mode are set before a fight so the mark is clear against the sky.

templates.text: "{name}" belongs to the radio, for talking to other aircraft and to the ground.
templates.context: Pilots tune it to the right station before flight and use it all the time to talk.

templates.text: "{name}" helps with navigation: knowing which way the aircraft flies and how to reach the next point.
templates.context: Pilots set it up before flight and check it often on the way.

templates.text: "{name}" belongs to the autopilot, which can hold the aircraft's height, heading or path by itself.
templates.context: Pilots switch it on for long, calm parts of a flight and off for take-off, landing and fights.

templates.text: "{name}" switches lights: lights outside so others see the aircraft, or lights inside so the pilot sees the instruments.
templates.context: Outside lights are on at night and near airfields; panel lights are dimmed so they do not dazzle.

templates.text: "{name}" opens or closes the cockpit's glass roof or a door.
templates.context: It is closed before take-off and opened after landing; in an emergency some canopies can be thrown off.

templates.text: "{name}" belongs to the escape system that gets the pilot out of the aircraft in an emergency.
templates.context: It is only used when the aircraft cannot be saved.

templates.text: "{name}" belongs to the breathing system: high up the air is too thin to breathe, so the pilot gets oxygen.
templates.context: It is switched on before climbing high.

templates.text: "{name}" keeps ice and fog away from the wings, the windows or the measuring tubes, by heating them or wiping them.
templates.context: It is switched on in cold, wet weather and clouds.

templates.text: "{name}" releases decoys that fool enemy missiles: hot flares against heat-seeking missiles, chaff (metal strips) against radar missiles.
templates.context: Pilots release them when a missile is coming.

templates.text: "{name}" belongs to the sensors that find targets and other aircraft, like a radar or a targeting camera.
templates.context: Pilots use it to find, follow and pick targets.

templates.text: "{name}" is an instrument: it shows the pilot a number or a needle, such as speed, height, engine temperature or time.
templates.context: Pilots glance at their instruments all the time to know how the aircraft and its engine are doing.

templates.text: "{name}" is a screen that shows the pilot pictures and information, such as a map, the radar or the weapons.
templates.context: Pilots switch its pages with the buttons around it or with their hands-on controls.

templates.text: "{name}" belongs to the ship's systems: its shields, its fast-travel drive or its thrusters.
templates.context: These are part of the game's spacecraft and work as the game describes them.

templates.text: "{name}" is a help for seeing better, a mirror, a view or a simulator helper, not part of flying itself.
templates.context: It makes the game easier to use and does not change how the aircraft flies.
